k: gabriel faure john singer sargent · 1889 sargent was a pianist as well as a painter, knew faure personally and helped introduce his music to english musical circles. this portrait records their working friendship. the dark suit and almost unpainted background concentrate attention on the head: compare the social setting of faure’s songs with the density of the musical argument they accommodated.

title: Mezzetin
k: mezzetin antoine watteau · c. 1718–20 mezzetin, a stock lover of the commedia dell’arte, sings to a guitar in a park while a marble woman turns her back on him. this is the world verlaine took from watteau for fetes galantes (1869): the “masques et bergamasques, jouant du luth” of clair de lune, which faure set in 1887 (op. 46 no. 2) with a minuet in the piano that carries on regardless of the voice. the link runs through the poem’s ancestry; a direct source for the song remains undocumented.

title: Clair de lune
sub: Paul Verlaine · 1869; set by Fauré in 1887
k: clair de lune paul verlaine · 1869; set by faure in 1887 faure’s setting, op. 46 no. 2, begins with a piano introduction long enough to establish the dance before the singer enters. debussy set the same poem twice and later used its title for a piano piece. the text names the minor mode; its central contradiction lies between an enacted happiness and the dancers’ disbelief.

title: Poster for the Moravian Teachers’ Choir
k: poster for the moravian teachers’ choir alfons mucha · 1911 mucha’s woman in moravian dress listens to a bird. the poster advertises the moravian teachers’ choir, a male-voice ensemble under ferdinand vach and an important interpreter of janacek’s demanding choral music. folk culture, organised amateur singing and contemporary composition meet in this institution. the mucha foundation’s catalogue identifies the costume with the kyjov region.

title: Illustration for the ninth instalment of Liška Bystrouška
k: illustration for the ninth instalment of liska bystrouska stanislav lolek · 16 april 1920 lolek’s drawings prompted rudolf tesnohlidek’s newspaper narrative, which in turn supplied janacek with the cunning little vixen. the composer changed the narrative and its ending, placing the forester’s recognition of recurring life after the vixen’s death. the printed drawing preserves the comic, observed animal world from which that operatic structure grew.

title: Near the Malvern Hills
sub: John Joseph Barker · Nineteenth century; undated
k: near the malvern hills john joseph barker · nineteenth century; undated the malvern ridge belongs to elgar’s working geography: he lived at malvern link during the years leading to enigma, walked in the hills and later cycled through worcestershire. barker’s painting shares that terrain, with no documented connection to a particular composition. its cultivated foreground recalls the inhabited countryside on which elgar’s musical life depended: nearby households, churches, schools and amateur players.

title: The Dream of Gerontius — the Angel’s farewell
k: the dream of gerontius — the angel’s farewell john henry newman · 1865 these are the opening two stanzas of the angel’s final song: the water is purgatory, and the separation is temporary. elgar sets the farewell in d major, with the mezzo-soprano’s line supported by a restrained orchestral texture. the poem’s repeated actions — holding, lowering, releasing — give the final scene its measured pace. newman’s text supplies the theological detail that concert extracts often lose.

title: The Latin Quarter: set design for La bohème, Act II
k: the latin quarter: set design for la boheme, act ii adolfo hohenstein · 1896 hohenstein designed the setting for the first production at turin’s teatro regio on 1 february 1896. the crowded square is part of the composition’s working apparatus: cafe tables, street traffic, vendors and a passing military band must be visible or audible in relation to one another. puccini’s separate musical groups inhabit the spaces that the designer provides.

title: Scènes de la vie de bohème — preface
k: scenes de la vie de boheme — preface henry murger · 1851 murger names three possible destinations, only one of them success. puccini’s librettists compressed characters and incidents from the stories and their theatrical adaptation. the final act makes the hospital-and-morgue possibilities concrete, giving the preface’s satire a tragic weight. the original preface sets out the stakes of “bohemian” life.

title: Wie die Thiere den Jäger begraben (How the Animals Bury the Hunter)
k: wie die thiere den jager begraben (how the animals bury the hunter) moritz von schwind · 1850 a children’s picture-sheet from munich: hares carry banners, a fox weeps, deer and boars follow the coffin of the hunter who used to shoot them. mahler cited this kind of image — an old austrian nursery print — as the seed of the funeral march in the first symphony. it explains the movement’s tone exactly: a procession that is both mournful and absurd, with a klezmer-like band (oboes, e♭ clarinets, bass drum with cymbal attached) breaking in on the solemnity.

title: Beethoven Frieze: This Kiss to the Whole World
k: beethoven frieze: this kiss to the whole world gustav klimt · 1902 klimt painted the frieze for the vienna secession’s 1902 exhibition in honour of beethoven, as a visual reading of the ninth symphony’s finale; its last panel takes its title from schiller’s ode to joy. at the opening, mahler conducted his own arrangement of a passage from that finale for wind instruments. the armoured knight on the frieze’s long wall has often been said to carry mahler’s features — an attribution that cannot be proved, but tells you how vienna saw its opera director.

title: Attersee
k: attersee gustav klimt · 1900 the lake where mahler built his first composing hut, at steinbach, and wrote the second and third symphonies (1893–96). klimt summered there from 1900 and painted it on square canvases, cropping the horizon almost out of the picture until the water becomes a field of colour. when the conductor bruno walter visited steinbach and stared at the mountains, mahler told him not to bother: “i have already composed all that.”

title: Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen
sub: Friedrich Rückert · c. 1821; set by Mahler 1901
k: ich bin der welt abhanden gekommen friedrich ruckert · c. 1821; set by mahler 1901 the middle stanza is omitted here. mahler set the poem in f major for voice and a reduced orchestra, with the cor anglais carrying a line that seems to grow out of the voice. he said of it: “it is my very self.” the adagietto of the fifth symphony, composed the same summer, is in the same key and breathes the same air.

title: Der Abschied — closing lines
k: der abschied — closing lines gustav mahler, after hans bethge · 1908 bethge’s die chinesische flote (1907) gave mahler loose german paraphrases of tang poets — li bai, wang wei, meng haoran — already filtered through french and german translations. for the end of der abschied mahler stopped adapting and wrote these lines himself.

title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
k: under the wave off kanagawa katsushika hokusai · c. 1830–32 debussy chose an adaptation of hokusai’s wave for the cover of durand’s 1905 edition of la mer. the printed score isolates and stylises the wave from the view shown here. the score’s subtitle remains ‘three symphonic sketches’.

title: Nocturne: Blue and Silver — Chelsea
k: nocturne: blue and silver — chelsea james mcneill whistler · 1871 whistler’s series of painted nocturnes supplied debussy with a model for the title of his orchestral triptych. whistler had borrowed a musical genre-name to direct attention towards arrangements of colour; debussy took it back with that pictorial implication. this thames view represents the series.

title: L’Après-midi d’un faune — opening
k: l’apres-midi d’un faune — opening stephane mallarme · 1876 the faun’s memory blurs encounter and invention. in debussy’s prelude, the returning flute phrase acquires changing harmonic contexts. mallarme attended the 1894 premiere and wrote his approval to debussy afterwards. the excerpt preserves the opening’s interrupted syntax.

title: Impression, soleil levant
k: impression, soleil levant claude monet · 1872 the title of monet’s le havre harbour painting helped give impressionism its name after the 1874 exhibition. debussy was repeatedly placed under that label. compare the few dark boats that establish distance against the harbour’s coloured marks with the separation of rhythmic layers in la mer.

title: Also sprach Zarathustra — Zarathustra’s prologue, §1
k: also sprach zarathustra — zarathustra’s prologue, §1 friedrich nietzsche · 1883 zarathustra addresses the sun before descending from his mountain solitude. strauss’s orchestral sunrise makes the address audible; later section headings draw on other chapters. nietzsche’s metaphor gives a reason for the opening’s direction, from a low pedal to a high brass declaration. the german text supplies the source.

title: Judith II (Salome)
k: judith ii (salome) gustav klimt · 1909 the painting’s alternative title records the period’s tendency to confuse judith, who kills holofernes, with salome, who demands jochanaan’s head. strauss’s opera concerns the latter. both belong to the same early-twentieth-century reconsideration of the biblical woman holding a severed male head. the date also coincides with elektra: classical and biblical subjects were being detached from reassuring academic conventions.

title: Der Rosenkavalier — the Marschallin on time
k: der rosenkavalier — the marschallin on time hugo von hofmannsthal · 1911 the act i speech is written for a woman who understands that her young lover will leave her. strauss largely withdraws the conversational bustle around the marschallin, giving her words room within an orchestral continuity that does not stop. hofmannsthal turns the passing of time into the comedy’s subject; the final trio will make her act upon the knowledge expressed here. the german libretto preserves the speech in its theatrical context.

title: Lemminkäinen’s Mother
k: lemminkainen’s mother akseli gallen-kallela · 1897 in the kalevala, lemminkainen is killed during his attempt to shoot the swan of tuonela; his mother gathers the dismembered body and restores him to life. gallen-kallela paints the body beside the river, with the swan in the distance. sibelius’s lemminkainen in tuonela treats the same narrative world. the picture postdates the legends’ first performance; a shared text and an artistic friendship connect the works.

title: Symposium
k: symposium akseli gallen-kallela · 1894 from left to right: gallen-kallela, oskar merikanto, robert kajanus and sibelius. the group met in helsinki, notably at the hotel kamp, and discussed music and the other arts. kajanus’s practical advocacy mattered as much as the conversation: he conducted sibelius’s works and later recorded several symphonies. the painting places the composer within a sociable, metropolitan artistic circle.

title: Kullervo Cursing
k: kullervo cursing akseli gallen-kallela · 1899 kullervo raises his fist after breaking his inherited knife on a stone baked into his bread. this episode precedes the incest and suicide central to sibelius’s five-movement work. the painting supplies narrative context. both artists shape the kalevala into modern works with individual formal decisions.

title: Portrait d’Erik Satie
k: portrait d’erik satie suzanne valadon · 1893 valadon painted satie during their brief relationship in montmartre. her outline fixes the head and narrow torso against a plain background, without a piano or other professional attribute. the picture records a relationship between two working artists. she died in 1938, and the painting is in the public domain.

title: Le Pauvre pêcheur
k: le pauvre pecheur pierre puvis de chavannes · 1881 satie admired puvis de chavannes; the painter’s restricted colour, flattened space and restrained gestures provide an artistic context for his preference for reduced means. the link is to the painter’s work generally; this canvas is not named in the score of socrate. compare the separation of its figures and their restrained gestures with the work’s detached narration of socrates’s death.

title: Prometheus
k: prometheus jean delville · 1907 delville’s prometheus belongs to the belgian painter’s symbolist and theosophical interpretation of the myth: fire becomes an emblem of intellectual and spiritual illumination. scriabin knew delville, who designed the published score of prometheus. a shared intellectual circle and a documented collaboration connect the two artists.

title: Cover design for Prometheus: The Poem of Fire
k: cover design for prometheus: the poem of fire jean delville · 1911 the printed design places the score inside the same esoteric visual culture as delville’s painting. separate documents record the colour correspondences of the clavier a lumieres. scriabin’s system orders hues partly through the circle of fifths, while the score’s two light lines distinguish local harmonic change from larger formal spans. gawboy and townsend’s study compares sabaneev’s 1911 table with scriabin’s own 1913 annotations.

title: Die Toteninsel (Isle of the Dead), first version
k: die toteninsel (isle of the dead), first version arnold bocklin · 1880 a boat bearing a white figure and coffin approaches rock, cypresses and openings cut into the island. bocklin made five versions between 1880 and 1886; this is the first, in basel. rachmaninoff encountered the image through a black-and-white reproduction in paris in 1907; which version it reproduced remains uncertain. his 1909 symphonic poem translates the approach into a repeated 5/8 figure.

title: Rachmaninoff with family and friends at Ivanovka
k: rachmaninoff with family and friends at ivanovka unidentified photographer · mid-1890s rachmaninoff stands second from the left in the back row. this is the satin family’s estate near tambov, where he first spent a summer in 1890 and returned to compose before 1917. the photograph places the music within the household where he worked. ivanovka provided the working conditions for the first concerto and much of the third; it was also a farm on which he spent substantial earnings.

title: Portrait of Sergei Rachmaninoff
k: portrait of sergei rachmaninoff konstantin somov · 1925 somov, a member of the mir iskusstva circle, painted rachmaninoff during his own years abroad. the frontal head, dark coat and restrained background present the professional musician without a piano or score. its date falls between the establishment of rachmaninoff’s american touring career and his return to major composition with the fourth concerto in 1926.

title: The Bells — opening section
k: the bells — opening section edgar allan poe · 1849 rachmaninoff set konstantin balmont’s russian adaptation of poe’s english in op. 35. the four-part sequence remains, from these sleigh bells through wedding and alarm bells to the iron funeral bell. repeated words already behave as rhythmic cells; rachmaninoff gives repetition to the chorus and orchestral accompaniment as well as the soloist. the complete poem was published in 1849, after poe’s death.

title: Не пой, красавица, при мне… (Do not sing, beautiful one, before me)
k: не пои, красавица, при мне… (do not sing, beautiful one, before me) alexander pushkin · 1828; set by rachmaninoff 1892 the first two of four stanzas. rachmaninoff set the complete poem as op. 4 no. 4, in a minor, and dedicated the song to natalia satina. the piano’s introduction establishes the returning music before the singer asks not to hear it: memory has already entered the room. the poem predates rachmaninoff’s exile by almost ninety years, and his setting by twenty-five.

title: Snap the Whip
k: snap the whip winslow homer · 1872 homer’s boys play a chain game outside a rural schoolhouse in the years after the civil war. ives’s childhood in danbury supplied comparable games, parades and community music-making for later scores, including the child’s outing in putnam’s camp. the link is shared subject matter; there is no evidence ives used this painting as a source. homer’s strained line of connected bodies offers a visual counterpart to coordinated activity that threatens to pull apart.

title: Self-Reliance — excerpt
k: self-reliance — excerpt ralph waldo emerson · 1841 the opening movement of the concord sonata is named for emerson, and ives discusses his writing at length in essays before a sonata. ives’s themes interrupt and qualify one another, as arguments do in the essays, finding continuity in their exchanges. this is prose, line-broken here for reading.

title: Walden, “Sounds” — excerpt
k: walden, “sounds” — excerpt henry david thoreau · 1854 the concord sonata’s last movement concerns thoreau at walden and includes an optional flute, the instrument thoreau himself played. this passage compares mechanical and natural sound while keeping their sources distinct. ives similarly lets a church bell, hymn or march retain its character within an outdoor setting. the excerpt is prose.

title: Blue Self-Portrait
k: blue self-portrait arnold schoenberg · 1910 schoenberg painted this small frontal self-portrait during the period of op. 11 and erwartung. colour alters the face without eliminating it: the blue surface is still organised around eyes, nose and mouth. his first exhibition took place in vienna in 1910, and four paintings appeared in the first blaue reiter exhibition in 1911. commons identifies this reproduction as public domain; schoenberg’s works entered the public domain in life-plus-seventy-year jurisdictions in 2022.

title: The Schoenberg Family
k: the schoenberg family richard gerstl · 1908 gerstl painted arnold, mathilde and their children during his association with the family. broad brushmarks break up the conventional portrait group; the figures remain present without precise facial description. his affair with mathilde and his suicide in november 1908 coincide with the second string quartet’s completion and first performance. the connection is biographical.

title: Composition V
k: composition v wassily kandinsky · 1911 kandinsky began corresponding with schoenberg after a munich concert in january 1911. this large canvas was exhibited with the first blaue reiter exhibition, where schoenberg’s paintings also appeared. its residual last judgement imagery is broken into lines and colour masses. the parallel lies in the pair’s debate about inherited artistic rules.

title: Mondestrunken
sub: Albert Giraud, German version by Otto Erich Hartleben · French original 1884; German version 1892
k: mondestrunken albert giraud, german version by otto erich hartleben · french original 1884; german version 1892 the first two stanzas of the opening poem in pierrot lunaire. hartleben’s german freely reworks giraud. the repeated opening lines belong to the poem’s rondel construction; schoenberg varies their musical setting. verbal recurrence and musical variation are deliberately separated.

title: Set design for Act I of Daphnis et Chloé
k: set design for act i of daphnis et chloe leon bakst · 1912 bakst designed the scenery and costumes for the ballets russes production of ravel’s ballet, choreographed by fokine and first performed in paris in june 1912. the drawing’s antiquity is a stage construction: monumental landscape surrounds the space in which human figures move. ravel’s wordless chorus and slowly accumulated orchestral layers create a corresponding scale. harvard identifies this sheet as act i.

title: Ondine — opening and closing paragraphs
sub: Aloysius Bertrand · 1842; text from the 1895 edition
k: ondine — opening and closing paragraphs aloysius bertrand · 1842; text from the 1895 edition the intervening paragraphs, in which ondine describes her underwater palace and proposes marriage, are omitted. bertrand’s gaspard de la nuit was published posthumously in 1842; ravel’s 1908 piano triptych prints its three source poems. the first movement must distinguish the water’s continuous motion from the spirit’s song, then accommodate her laughter and disappearance. the french follows the 1895 mercure de france edition; the translation here is our own.

title: Le Petit Poucet: the children at the ogre’s door
k: le petit poucet: the children at the ogre’s door gustave dore · 1867 edition the lantern isolates seven children beneath the ogre’s house; the architectural scale makes their physical vulnerability measurable. ravel’s petit poucet, the second piece of ma mere l’oye, uses the same perrault tale but an earlier incident: the lost breadcrumb trail. wandering lines and changing bar lengths replace a secure processional pulse; birds enter the orchestral version as instrumental calls. the link with dore is the shared text.

title: Court Ball in Vienna
k: court ball in vienna wilhelm gause · 1900 ravel planned a homage to johann strauss as early as 1906, provisionally titled wien; he finished it after the war, in 1919–20, as la valse. gause’s view of a habsburg court ball — chandeliers, uniforms, a floor packed with turning couples — is the scene the score’s preface names. what ravel did to it is the point: the waltz is assembled from fragments emerging out of murk in the double basses, built to a brilliant climax, and then driven past it until the three-beat metre breaks apart.

title: Preface to the score of La Valse
k: preface to the score of la valse maurice ravel · 1920 ravel printed this scenario at the head of the score of his “poeme choregraphique”. it is also a set of orchestration instructions in disguise: the clouds are the muted, divided double basses that open the piece; the gaps are the first waltz fragments surfacing in the bassoons; “eclate au ff” marks the exact dynamic at which the full orchestra arrives. ravel insisted the setting was 1855, not 1914 — but the score’s violent ending has been heard as an epitaph for that court ever since.

title: Bartók recording Slovak folk songs at Zobordarázs
k: bartok recording slovak folk songs at zobordarazs photographer unidentified · 1907 the phonograph horn makes the act of collection visible: a particular singer performs for a recording machine while other villagers gather nearby. zobordarazs is now drazovce, slovakia. the bartok archives dates this photograph to 1907, rather than the 1908 supplied in the commons metadata. pair it with the slovak volumes of for children: the compositional source is a performed and variable melody.

title: Bartók during his first Transylvanian collecting trip
k: bartok during his first transylvanian collecting trip istvan kovats · 1907 kovats photographed bartok at gyergyoszentmiklos, now gheorgheni, during the collecting expedition of 1907. this identification follows the archive’s 2022 exhibition catalogue, rather than commons’ approximate 1903 date. the trip’s pentatonic hungarian songs belong to the documented background of the stylistic change around the fourteen bagatelles and first quartet.

title: The Lonely Cedar
k: the lonely cedar tivadar csontvary kosztka · 1907 csontvary, who died in 1919, painted a lebanese cedar. the hungarian painter’s foreign subject shows the reach of his material beyond his own country. beside bartok’s night music, the isolated branching form and broad background offer a comparison of foreground and field. the pairing is visual, with no claim of musical influence. the national gallery catalogue records the canvas and its date.

title: Ruins of the Greek Theatre at Taormina
k: ruins of the greek theatre at taormina tivadar csontvary kosztka · 1904–05 the theatre’s masonry establishes a close, articulated foreground against sea, coast and mountain. paired with music for strings, percussion and celesta, it invites comparison between a large design and the separate planes through which that design becomes perceptible. csontvary was an older hungarian contemporary working outside academic naturalism; the link here is formal, with no documented connection to the score.

title: Kiss to the Earth: second variant of the scenery design for The Rite of Spring
k: kiss to the earth: second variant of the scenery design for the rite of spring nicholas roerich · 1912 roerich was the ballet’s co-author as well as its designer. this study belongs to the 1913 production’s first part, “adoration of the earth”; its receding hills and stones place collective action in a landscape. the scenario’s games, processions and sacrifice supplied occasions for contrasted musical blocks. roerich’s archaeological interests informed these modern constructions of pagan ceremony. commons identifies this pre-1931 design as public domain; roerich died in 1947.

title: Costume design for The Firebird
k: costume design for the firebird leon bakst · 1910 bakst’s design belongs to the ballets russes production that introduced stravinsky to paris. its elaborated wings and plumage made the supernatural creature visible through a dancer’s body; the score distinguishes that creature through chromatic movement, rapid figuration and orchestral colour. the production was collaborative: fokine choreographed, alexander golovin designed the scenery and other costumes, and karsavina created the firebird.

title: Tsarevich Ivan and the Firebird
sub: Ivan Bilibin · 1899, dated in the image
k: tsarevich ivan and the firebird ivan bilibin · 1899, dated in the image bilibin shows ivan catching a feather from the bird among the apple trees, a scene from the tale of ivan tsarevich, the firebird and the grey wolf. the ballet’s scenario combines material from several russian tales. the illustration establishes the existing visual vocabulary — the bird’s long plumage, the orchard, ivan’s clothing — on which a paris audience’s russian fairy-tale spectacle depended. it belongs to the source tradition, outside the designs for the 1910 production.

title: A Rake’s Progress, Plate VIII: In Bedlam
k: a rake’s progress, plate viii: in bedlam william hogarth · 1735 stravinsky saw hogarth’s series in chicago in 1947 and proposed it as an opera subject. this final plate supplies the destination, bedlam; auden and kallman added nick shadow and the pact with the devil. hogarth’s sequential scenes find a musical counterpart in the opera’s separate arias, ensembles and recitatives. the closing epilogue, delivered outside the action, restores the moral address to an audience that the prints make through their captions and details.

title: Nature, central panel of the Alpine Triptych
k: nature, central panel of the alpine triptych giovanni segantini · 1897–99 webern’s plan for his unnumbered string quartet of 1905 refers to segantini’s triptych, whose panels were known to him as werden, sein and vergehen — becoming, being and passing away. this central panel places cattle and figures within the engadine mountains at sunset. the documented connection belongs to that early work’s conception.

title: Abendland II
sub: Georg Trakl · Published in Sebastian im Traum, 1915; set by Webern 1919
k: abendland ii georg trakl · published in sebastian im traum, 1915; set by webern 1919 webern set this as the third of the six songs, op. 14, for voice, clarinet, violin and cello. trakl’s clauses move from homeland to ruined wall, vineyard and eagles, leaving the connections unstated. the score gives those transitions space through sparse instrumental entries. the german is the version used in the song; the english here is a new translation.

title: Portrait of Alban Berg
k: portrait of alban berg arnold schoenberg · 1910 schoenberg painted his pupil in the year of the string quartet, op. 3. the tall, narrow canvas belongs to the teacher’s concentrated period of portrait painting; it depicts a working relationship that began with harmony lessons in 1904 and continued after berg’s operatic success.

title: De profundis clamavi — opening quatrain
sub: Charles Baudelaire · 1857; text from the 1861 edition
k: de profundis clamavi — opening quatrain charles baudelaire · 1857; text from the 1861 edition the finale of the lyric suite conceals a setting of this poem in stefan george’s german translation. berg’s annotated copy for hanna fuchs-robettin supplied the evidence discovered by george perle in 1977. the french original appears here. its address to one absent beloved explains the vocal conception behind the instrumental lament.

title: Romeo and Juliet
k: romeo and juliet frank dicksee · 1884 dicksee and prokofiev work from the same shakespeare play. the painting concentrates the lovers’ encounter into an embrace on the balcony; the ballet gives the encounter a sequence of approaches, withdrawals and sustained phrases. compare the image with the end of act i. the contrast between the private meeting and the capulets’ public ceremonial behaviour, heard in the knights’ dance usually detached from the score, is already built into shakespeare’s arrangement of scenes.

title: Fix Bayonets! Hurrah! Hurrah! (The Attack)
k: fix bayonets! hurrah! hurrah! (the attack) vasily vereshchagin · 1887–95 one of vereshchagin’s napoleon i in russia paintings, dealing with the same 1812 campaign that occupies the war scenes of prokofiev’s opera. the advancing soldiers fill the foreground, bringing the viewer into the movement of bodies. the link is the campaign; use of the canvas as a source is undocumented. set it beside the opera’s borodino scene and tolstoy’s insistence that no general can encompass a battle’s simultaneous actions.

title: Cinderella
k: cinderella gustave dore · 1867 edition dore’s illustration belongs to an edition of perrault’s tales; nikolai volkov also used perrault for the scenario of prokofiev’s cinderella. the shared source matters because the fairy’s transformation, the ball and the time limit require different kinds of stage time. prokofiev gives each a musical mechanism: changes of orchestral colour for transformation, extended dances for the ball, and repeated clock figures for the limit.

title: Idols, sketch
k: idols, sketch nicholas roerich · 1901 roerich’s fenced sanctuary belongs to his imagined ancient rus. he later devised the scenario and designs for stravinsky’s the rite of spring; diaghilev’s subsequent prehistoric commission to prokofiev produced ala and lolli and, after its rejection, the scythian suite. the link is the ballets russes interest in a reconstructed pagan past. roerich’s repeated posts and carved figures offer a visual counterpart to the suite’s blocks of repeated rhythm.

title: War and Peace: Natasha at the window
sub: Leo Tolstoy · 1865–69; Volume II, Part III, Chapter II
k: war and peace: natasha at the window leo tolstoy · 1865–69; volume ii, part iii, chapter ii prince andrei hears this conversation without the women knowing he is below their window. prokofiev and mira mendelson made the otradnoye episode the opera’s opening scene: natasha’s delight reaches a listener within the drama before it reaches us as an operatic declaration. the extract gives tolstoy’s prose, with paragraphing from the russian virtual library text.

title: Lili and Nadia Boulanger
k: lili and nadia boulanger agence meurisse · 1913 the photograph belongs to the press coverage surrounding lili’s prix de rome. it places the sisters in the same documentary frame before nadia’s long teaching career made her the better-known name. their musical collaboration was practical: study, performance, copying and, at the end of lili’s life, dictation. the surviving scores distinguish two composing careers.

title: Elle était descendue
sub: Francis Jammes · From Tristesses, 1906; set in 1913–14
k: elle etait descendue francis jammes · from tristesses, 1906; set in 1913–14 the first song of clairieres dans le ciel begins with this precise memory: wet plants, an awkward movement, a gaze. jammes describes the meadow twice as the speaker returns to it. boulanger’s cycle similarly allows remembered musical material to return with altered significance. jammes died in 1938; this is the public-domain french original with a new translation.

title: Le Groupe des Six
k: le groupe des six jacques-emile blanche · 1922 blanche’s portrait of the circle includes the pianist marcelle meyer and jean cocteau as well as composers. it records a network of performers, writers and friends. poulenc’s study with koechlin supplied private technical discipline behind that sociable public image.

title: Le Dromadaire, from Le Bestiaire
k: le dromadaire, from le bestiaire raoul dufy · 1911 apollinaire’s poems were published with dufy’s woodcuts before poulenc selected six of them in 1919. the book joins animal image and compressed verbal form. compare the print’s bounded black-and-white shapes with the song’s short phrases: both work at a scale that makes every addition conspicuous.

title: Le Dromadaire
sub: Guillaume Apollinaire · 1911; set by Poulenc in 1919
k: le dromadaire guillaume apollinaire · 1911; set by poulenc in 1919 the first of poulenc’s six bestiaire songs retains the poem’s disproportionately grand traveller and its modest conditional ending within the compass of apollinaire’s five lines. he died in 1918, and the 1911 original is public domain; the english translation here is new.

title: Portrait of Mitya Shostakovich
k: portrait of mitya shostakovich boris kustodiev · 1919 kustodiev drew shostakovich in the year he entered the petrograd conservatory and inscribed the portrait to his young friend. the memorial apartment’s catalogue distinguishes this 1919 drawing from a second portrait made at gaspra in 1923; the reproduced commons file is the earlier work. it documents an actual connection with the painter, before the first symphony made the student an internationally performed composer.

title: Anti-aircraft guns near St Isaac’s Cathedral, Leningrad
k: anti-aircraft guns near st isaac’s cathedral, leningrad boris kudoyarov · 24 november 1941 kudoyarov photographed an anti-aircraft battery firing beside st isaac’s during the siege. shostakovich had already been evacuated and was completing the seventh symphony in kuibyshev; the picture records the city to which he dedicated it. the symphony was performed inside leningrad on 9 august 1942. commons identifies this file as public domain under its russian archival-rights declaration.

title: The Nose — the nose refuses its owner
k: the nose — the nose refuses its owner nikolai gogol · 1836 in the cathedral encounter, kovalyov’s nose defeats his claim through the language of official rank and departmental boundaries. shostakovich’s opera preserves that collision between an impossible event and exact bureaucratic procedure, giving the nose a tenor voice and kovalyov a baritone. the extract follows the russian text in the academy of sciences collected edition; the english translation is ours. leskov provides the separate source for lady macbeth of the mtsensk district.

title: Wood Thrush, plate 73 of The Birds of America
sub: Robert Havell after John James Audubon · 1829
k: wood thrush, plate 73 of the birds of america robert havell after john james audubon · 1829 the wood thrush, hylocichla mustelina, is messiaen’s grive des bois. it supplies the title and musical material of movement ten of des canyons aux etoiles…. the work’s commentary describes its clear major arpeggio and lower rustling aftermath. havell’s plate after audubon identifies the same bird visually, beside flowering dogwood. the pairing rests on the shared species. the nineteenth-century artwork is public domain; the national gallery’s scan is released under cc0.

title: The Mocking Bird, plate 21 of The Birds of America
sub: Robert Havell after John James Audubon · 1827
k: the mocking bird, plate 21 of the birds of america robert havell after john james audubon · 1827 movement nine of des canyons aux etoiles…, le moqueur polyglotte, gives the northern mockingbird an unaccompanied piano movement. short calls, trills and repeated-note figures make one instrument carry a changing repertory of gestures. audubon’s birds confront a snake at their nest. the connection is the identified species and the act of detailed observation. like the wood-thrush plate, this public-domain engraving is available as a cc0 national gallery scan.

title: Revelation 10:1, 5–6 — the angel’s oath
sub: John of Patmos; Latin Vulgate tradition · First century CE; Clementine Vulgate edition, 1598
k: revelation 10:1, 5–6 — the angel’s oath john of patmos; latin vulgate tradition · first century ce; clementine vulgate edition, 1598 the angel, rainbow and oath in this biblical source supply the quartet’s programme. verses 2–4 are omitted, with the break shown above; the latin follows the public-domain clementine vulgate. ‘no more time’ translates the wording literally and follows messiaen’s musical reading of it; the passage is also understood as announcing no further delay before fulfilment. slow louanges and rhythmic palindromes make that interpretation audible without a sung text.

title: Judith and Job window, Sainte-Chapelle
sub: Thirteenth-century Parisian glass painters; photograph by Yair Haklai · c. 1248, with later restorations; photographed 12 April 2017
k: judith and job window, sainte-chapelle thirteenth-century parisian glass painters; photograph by yair haklai · c. 1248, with later restorations; photographed 12 april 2017 messiaen visited the sainte-chapelle as a child and repeatedly connected its coloured light with his musical thinking. et exspecto resurrectionem mortuorum received its first performance here on 7 may 1965 under serge baudo. this photograph shows the judith and job bay within the chapel’s medieval biblical glazing. the image is by yair haklai, licensed cc by-sa 4.0. medieval glass and later restoration coexist in the present window.

title: The Borough, Letter XXII — Peter Grimes
k: the borough, letter xxii — peter grimes george crabbe · 1810 crabbe was born in aldeburgh in 1754. these six lines describe grimes seeking out the estuary after the deaths of his apprentices; spelling is modernised. the poem supplies the opera’s subject. slater and britten shift its moral balance, giving grimes a capacity for imagination that crabbe’s sustained account of abuse scarcely permits. the water is already described through sound — a restricted, repetitive stream.

title: Anthem for Doomed Youth
k: anthem for doomed youth wilfred owen · 1917; published 1920 britten places this sonnet in the opening movement of the war requiem, giving it to the tenor and chamber orchestra. owen’s substitution of guns for bells and shells for a choir confronts the actual choir singing the requiem around him. the poem’s refusal of adequate funeral ritual interrupts the ritual being performed.

title: Golding Constable’s Kitchen Garden
k: golding constable’s kitchen garden john constable · c. 1815 constable paints the cultivated land behind his father’s house at east bergholt in suffolk. the connection is regional; there is no documented influence. britten’s aldeburgh music likewise belongs to a working county of gardens, churches, farms and fishing boats. read the ordered plots against crabbe’s estuary: both show a countryside shaped by human labour.

title: The Triumph of Death
k: the triumph of death pieter bruegel the elder · c. 1562 le grand macabre takes place in breughelland, the name inherited from michel de ghelderode’s play. bruegel’s crowded panorama offers a visual counterpart: soldiers, lovers, clergy and aristocrats occupy the same field while death overrides their distinctions. ligeti’s ending departs from its apparent finality: nekrotzar’s promised annihilation may have failed.

title: Lux aeterna
sub: Latin Requiem liturgy · Traditional Latin text; set by Ligeti in 1966
k: lux aeterna latin requiem liturgy · traditional latin text; set by ligeti in 1966 the communion text of the mass for the dead is the source of ligeti’s sixteen-part motet. its promise of light differs from the judgement imagery dominating his requiem. he repeats and overlaps its words, making individual syllables part of a shifting choral harmony before a whole phrase can be understood.

title: Polyphony
k: polyphony paul klee · 1932 boulez first encountered klee’s work in avignon in 1947 and returned to it in le pays fertile: paul klee (1989). klee’s dots, coloured fields and overlapping divisions make several organisations visible at once. boulez valued his demonstrations of how elementary operations can generate a complex form. the painting’s title names the musical analogy explicitly.

title: Une dentelle s’abolit
k: une dentelle s’abolit stephane mallarme · 1887 this sonnet supplies the text of ‘improvisation ii’, the central movement of pli selon pli. the mandore is a small plucked string instrument; the poem connects its hollow body with an absent bed and a possible birth. boulez stretches syllables and surrounds the soprano with instrumental resonance. the french follows the 1887 printed text; the translation retains its unresolved syntax.

title: Star Ushak Carpet
sub: Unidentified Anatolian weavers · Probably seventeenth century
k: star ushak carpet unidentified anatolian weavers · probably seventeenth century feldman collected middle eastern rugs and discussed their unequal repetitions in ‘crippled symmetry’ (1981). this anatolian carpet is not documented as one he owned. its repeating star medallions and bounded field make his comparison tangible: a motif can recur with changes to its intervals, contours or patches of colour. the met’s photograph is released under cc0.

title: Coptic Textile Fragment
sub: Unidentified Egyptian weavers · Late third–fifth century
k: coptic textile fragment unidentified egyptian weavers · late third–fifth century in his note for coptic light, feldman identifies ancient textiles at the louvre as a stimulus, asking how fragments can retain the character of the civilisation that made them. this met fragment offers a comparison. its surviving threads and colour boundaries suggest the persistence and renewal of instrumental colour in the orchestral work. the museum image is cc0.

title: Franz Kafka
k: franz kafka unknown photographer · 1923–24 kafka’s diaries, letters and notebooks supply the forty texts of kafka-fragmente. this late portrait belongs to the period before his death in 1924. kurtag’s work repeatedly changes the scale at which the writer is heard: an aphorism lasting seconds may stand beside a much longer scene for the same soprano and violin.

title: Die Guten gehn im gleichen Schritt
sub: Franz Kafka · Early twentieth century; set by Kurtág 1985–87
k: die guten gehn im gleichen schritt franz kafka · early twentieth century; set by kurtag 1985–87 the opening text of kafka-fragmente. its contrast is already musical: common step against surrounding dances. kurtag gives the soprano and violin distinct rhythmic behaviour. line breaks make kafka’s prose legible here.

title: An Zimmern
k: an zimmern friedrich holderlin · before 1812 ernst zimmer, the carpenter whose family cared for holderlin in tubingen, transmitted these four lines in 1812. kurtag sets them as the fourth of his holderlin-gesange, op. 35a, for unaccompanied baritone. the word “harmonies” is entrusted to one melodic line.

title: Crucifixion
k: crucifixion dionisius · 1500 the cross, the bowed figures and the narrow vertical field organise the icon before individual facial expressions are read. gubaidulina’s seven words treats the same subject through seven instrumental movements; in croce makes a crossing of registers into a formal event. the link is a shared christian tradition.

title: De profundis
sub: Psalm 130, verses 1–3; Latin Vulgate · Ancient psalm; late-antique Latin version
k: de profundis psalm 130, verses 1–3; latin vulgate · ancient psalm; late-antique latin version numbered 129 in the vulgate and 130 in the hebrew tradition, this psalm supplies the title of gubaidulina’s 1978 bayan piece. its first movement is verbal: a voice calls upwards from below. her instrumental register and the audible labour of the bellows translate that relation into sound.

title: The Trinity
k: the trinity andrei rublev · c. 1425–27 three angels sit around one table; repeated outlines and inclined heads bind distinct figures into a single composition. the icon belongs to the orthodox tradition part entered in 1972. the comparison is theological and formal: a restricted set of elements carries distinctions through placement and relation.

title: Da pacem Domine
k: da pacem domine anonymous latin antiphon · ninth century jordi savall commissioned part’s setting in 2004; part began it two days after the madrid train bombings of 11 march. the prayer’s compact clauses support a four-part texture whose sustained lines move at different rates. the old liturgical words address a particular recent event.

title: Pennsylvania Railroad train leaving Union Station, Chicago
k: pennsylvania railroad train leaving union station, chicago jack delano · january 1943 delano’s government photograph records the american railway system at almost the same moment as reich’s childhood journeys of 1939–42. different trains returns to that passenger world through a governess’s memories, a pullman porter’s testimony and recorded train sounds, then places it against deportation trains in europe. the photograph supplies historical context.

title: The heavens tell
sub: Psalm 19, verses 2–3 in Hebrew numbering · Ancient Hebrew text
k: the heavens tell psalm 19, verses 2–3 in hebrew numbering · ancient hebrew text the opening words of tehillim; the first movement continues through verse 5. reich composed his own melodies. the hebrew syllables generate flexible rhythmic groupings, and the voices enter in canons. these verses pair one day with another and one night with another before the music makes its own overlapping statements.

title: The Veteran in a New Field
k: the veteran in a new field winslow homer · 1865 the discarded union army jacket and canteen identify homer’s reaper as a returning civil war soldier. painted in the year that whitman published drum-taps, the canvas transfers attention from battle to the work of a surviving body. the link with adams is shared subject matter: the war and its aftermath, which the wound-dresser approaches through bandages, amputations and bedside care.

title: The Wound-Dresser — excerpt
k: the wound-dresser — excerpt walt whitman · 1865; later revised these lines begin adams’s setting, though they occur well inside whitman’s poem. the omission removes the old narrator’s introductory account of being asked for war stories and starts with practical labour. the sequence of unequal phrases gives the baritone a different rhythmic task from the orchestra’s recurring figures; the repetitions enact the return to each patient.

title: Batter my heart, three-person’d God
k: batter my heart, three-person’d god john donne · published 1633 donne’s holy sonnet xiv supplies oppenheimer’s aria at the end of act i of doctor atomic. the poem asks for spiritual remaking through violent paradox; in the opera its language of breaking, burning and captivity is heard beside the impending test of an atomic weapon.

title: Lake Keitele
k: lake keitele akseli gallen-kallela · 1905 gallen-kallela paints the finnish lake as bands of reflection and disturbed water. the link is a shared physical environment, with no documented connection to a composition: saariaho repeatedly discussed the bodily effect of finland’s extreme seasonal changes of light. in this painting, small changes of surface divide a continuous field; in lichtbogen, changes inside sustained sounds articulate a form. the painting predates her birth by forty-seven years.

title: Lanquan li jorn son lonc e may — first stanza
k: lanquan li jorn son lonc e may — first stanza jaufre rudel · twelfth century the repeated de lonh is a formal device before it is a plot. saariaho returned to rudel in lonh for soprano and electronics (1996), then in l’amour de loin. this medieval lyric precedes maalouf’s modern libretto; its manuscript tradition contains variant spellings and readings. the occitan text supplies the stanza translated above.

title: Vida of Jaufre Rudel — opening
k: vida of jaufre rudel — opening anonymous · thirteenth-century biographical tradition the medieval prose biography continues with rudel’s voyage, illness and death in the countess’s arms. its author is separated from the troubadour by generations; the love story belongs to legend. maalouf and saariaho adopt this narrative as theatre, giving the unnamed countess the name clemence and the travelling pilgrim a central mediating role.

title: Ferdinand Courting Miranda, from The Tempest
k: ferdinand courting miranda, from the tempest william hogarth · c. 1736 hogarth gathers ferdinand, miranda, prospero, ariel and caliban into an imagined scene. the link is shakespeare’s act i; no influence on the score is documented. ades’s opera assigns this same set of relations distinct vocal registers and forms of musical agency. hogarth places a controlling father, an invisible musician and two lovers in a single artistic space.

title: Ariel’s song: Full fathom five
sub: William Shakespeare · The Tempest, c. 1610–11; printed 1623
k: ariel’s song: full fathom five william shakespeare · the tempest, c. 1610–11; printed 1623 ariel sings to ferdinand about his supposedly drowned father in act i, scene 2. meredith oakes rewrites shakespeare’s song for the opera. its dramatic function remains musical deception, bringing ferdinand towards miranda. the very high soprano register gives the voice an audible distance from ordinary human speech; the transformation in the poem has a counterpart in the treatment of the singer.

title: The School of Athens
k: the school of athens raphael · 1509–11 pythagoras sits in the lower-left foreground, writing beside a tablet of musical proportions. raphael placed the mathematical study of consonance among philosophy’s principal disciplines, more than two millennia after pythagoras. the vatican’s account identifies the interval under discussion as the diatessaron, the fourth. the fresco records a renaissance view of ancient theory.

title: Hildegard receiving a vision
sub: Anonymous Rupertsberg illuminator · Late twelfth century
k: hildegard receiving a vision anonymous rupertsberg illuminator · late twelfth century hildegard receives the fiery light of inspiration while a scribe records her words. the image belongs to the visual transmission of scivias, her account of visions completed in 1151. her songs and the musical drama ordo virtutum connect this visionary theology with the daily sung worship of her community. their single melodic lines articulate register, verbal emphasis and formal return on their own.

title: The Guidonian hand
k: the guidonian hand anonymous illuminator · 1274 the enlarged hand makes a human body into a diagram of pitch and solmisation. dating from more than two centuries after guido’s teaching, it records the method’s later use. the outer circle repeats the syllables that are distributed across the hand, giving the pupil two spatial routes through the same information.

title: Ut queant laxis — first stanza
sub: Traditionally attributed to Paul the Deacon · Eighth century
k: ut queant laxis — first stanza traditionally attributed to paul the deacon · eighth century the hymn asks john the baptist to release the singer’s voice from impediment. guido used the first syllables of its six half-lines as a ladder of pitches. the words are older than his teaching method; the authorship traditionally assigned to paul the deacon is not certain.

title: Opening of Pérotin’s Viderunt omnes
k: opening of perotin’s viderunt omnes anonymous parisian scribe · thirteenth century the florence manuscript is one of the principal witnesses to the notre-dame repertory. its written ligatures encode groups of notes. a later copy, the page records the work’s transmission.

title: Nature presents Sense, Rhetoric and Music to Machaut
k: nature presents sense, rhetoric and music to machaut anonymous french illuminator · fourteenth century the allegory belongs to the presentation of machaut as an author: nature supplies the faculties with which he makes poetry and music. his literary and musical works circulated together in carefully organised books. music stands beside rhetoric because machaut practised both.

title: The Ghent Altarpiece: Singing Angels
k: the ghent altarpiece: singing angels hubert and jan van eyck · 1432 the angels crowd around one book, their mouths opened differently as they sing. the panel belongs to the same early-fifteenth-century ecclesiastical culture in which dufay’s music circulated. its lectern and shared volume make the material conditions of choral reading visible. the facing musical panel gives their companions an organ and stringed instruments.

title: The Lute Player
k: the lute player caravaggio · c. 1595–96 the singer holds a lute while a violin and music books lie on the table. the painted notation includes madrigals by jacques arcadelt: repertory written for separate vocal parts could also belong to a singer’s instrumental practice. the presence of both lute and violin matters more than a general association with ‘music’: it places two different string technologies beside the printed song they could help perform. the metropolitan museum’s study of the related version examines the instruments and identifiable music.

title: Portrait identified as Claudio Monteverdi
k: portrait identified as claudio monteverdi bernardo strozzi · c. 1630 the sitter’s identification rests on comparison with the securely identified engraving published in the commemorative fiori poetici of 1644. the portrait is later than orfeo and belongs to the composer’s venetian decades. strozzi also worked in venice: painting and opera shared a city of commissioned portraits, church appointments and, from 1637, ticket-selling musical theatres.

title: The Concert
k: the concert gerard ter borch · c. 1675 the two halves of a continuo team in one room: a woman with her back to us plays a cello — a bowed instrument that can sustain a bass line — while another sits at a harpsichord, the instrument that turned a figured bass into chords. ter borch paints the satin and the scroll of the cello more carefully than any music on the desk; the picture records the instruments and the domestic setting of accompanied music.

title: Gradus ad Parnassum: title page
sub: Johann Joseph Fux; title-page designer uncredited · 1725
k: gradus ad parnassum: title page johann joseph fux; title-page designer uncredited · 1725 the title means “steps to parnassus”, the mountain associated with apollo and the muses. fux makes a classical ascent into a practical teaching sequence: the pupil adds rhythmic freedom only after learning to control the intervals between voices. the printed page belongs to the same instructional culture as the dialogue inside it.

title: Mime at the anvil
k: mime at the anvil arthur rackham · 1911 rackham’s illustration shows mime at work in the smithy of siegfried, act i. the scene belongs to an opera in which the sword’s musical history precedes its successful reforging: the audience has already heard its associations in earlier parts of the ring. a picture can show the workshop and the broken metal at once; the score can place the sword’s remembered past against the present action.

title: Madonna del Parto
k: madonna del parto piero della francesca · c. 1450–65 grisey explicitly based l’icone paradoxale (1992–94), for two women’s voices and divided orchestra, on this fresco. in his programme note he describes the opened tent and the opening of mary’s dress as nested spaces, and identifies the proportions 3:5:8:12 as temporal material. the voices use piero’s names and text from his perspective treatise. the approximate dating follows the monterchi museum.
