title: Corelli climbs Couperin’s Parnassus
k: corelli climbs couperin’s parnassus arcangelo corelli → francois couperin · documented ext couperin’s 1724 trio sonata gives corelli a programme in seven named movements: he petitions the muses, drinks at hippocrene, sleeps, and is placed beside apollo. the tribute is explicit in the work’s title and movement headings, rather than a resemblance retrospectively assigned by listeners. corelli’s instrumental music le parnasse, ou l’apotheose de corelli (1724)

title: Lully and Corelli reconcile on Parnassus
k: lully and corelli reconcile on parnassus jean-baptiste lully → francois couperin · documented ext in couperin’s 1725 instrumental homage, apollo persuades lully and corelli to unite french and italian tastes. two successive headings specify lully playing the subject with corelli accompanying, then corelli playing while lully accompanies: stylistic reconciliation becomes an audible exchange of roles. lully’s french instrumental style l’apotheose de lully (1725)

title: An inherited dance closes Vivaldi’s first opus
sub: La Folia tradition → Antonio Vivaldi · documented
k: an inherited dance closes vivaldi’s first opus la folia tradition → antonio vivaldi · documented ext vivaldi ended his first published collection of trio sonatas with variations on la folia for two violins and continuo. the opening adagio states the familiar d-minor melody before the changing tempi and figuration; the source is a shared tradition, not a tune invented by corelli. the late folia melody and harmonic scheme trio sonata in d minor, op. 1 no. 12, rv 63 (1705) la-folia

title: Voltaire supplies Rameau’s comédie-ballet
k: voltaire supplies rameau’s comedie-ballet voltaire → jean-philippe rameau · documented ext rameau supplied the music for voltaire’s la princesse de navarre in 1745. the comedie-ballet has an overture and three acts; its literary author is the same voltaire better known for philosophical prose, not an anonymous court librettist. voltaire, la princesse de navarre la princesse de navarre, rct 44 (1745)

title: Bach outstays his leave in Lübeck
sub: Dieterich Buxtehude → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: bach outstays his leave in lubeck dieterich buxtehude → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach obtained leave from his arnstadt post in 1705 to visit lubeck and hear buxtehude, but remained away into 1706. the subsequent consistory examination records bach’s explanation that he had travelled to learn things connected with his art: the encounter is supported by an employment dispute, not merely an influence legend. buxtehude’s organ playing in lubeck bach’s visit of 1705–06

title: Bach copies an Italian organ Mass collection
sub: Girolamo Frescobaldi → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: bach copies an italian organ mass collection girolamo frescobaldi → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach copied out frescobaldi’s fiori musicali, a collection organised around three organ masses rather than a modern keyboard suite. its chant-based kyrie versets, canzonas and ricercars offered a concrete written model of liturgical counterpoint; the consulted accounts establish the copying but not its exact date. fiori musicali (1635) bach’s study copy of fiori musicali

title: Bach writes out a French organ book
sub: Nicolas de Grigny → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: bach writes out a french organ book nicolas de grigny → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach made a copy of grigny’s premier livre d’orgue, containing an organ mass and settings of five hymns. this is a specific route by which french liturgical organ writing reached bach; it does not depend on claiming that the two composers ever met. premier livre d’orgue (1699; reissued 1711) bach’s copy of grigny’s organ collection

title: An ensemble sonata becomes a keyboard work
sub: Johann Adam Reincken → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: an ensemble sonata becomes a keyboard work johann adam reincken → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach’s a-minor keyboard sonata bwv 965 adapts reincken’s first sonata from hortus musicus, originally ensemble music. the keyboard version retains a succession of introductory, fugal and dance movements: the transmission is an identifiable arrangement, not simply membership of the north german organ school. hortus musicus, sonata no. 1 sonata in a minor, bwv 965 (c. 1705)

title: Two solo violins move onto Bach’s organ
sub: Antonio Vivaldi → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: two solo violins move onto bach’s organ antonio vivaldi → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach transcribed vivaldi’s a-minor concerto for two violins, strings and continuo as the solo-organ concerto bwv 593 around 1713. the two manuals let him distinguish tutti and solo material; added ornaments, middle-voice detail and fuller chords adapt the same concerto architecture to the organ. concerto in a minor, op. 3 no. 8, rv 522 (1711) organ concerto in a minor, bwv 593 (c. 1713)

title: Four violins become four harpsichords
sub: Antonio Vivaldi → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: four violins become four harpsichords antonio vivaldi → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach converted vivaldi’s b-minor concerto for four violins into an a-minor concerto for four harpsichords and strings. each violin line becomes a two-handed keyboard part; the broken-chord slow movement remains especially close to vivaldi’s original, despite the changed instrumental sound. concerto in b minor, op. 3 no. 10, rv 580 concerto for four harpsichords in a minor, bwv 1065 (c. 1730)

title: An oboe concerto becomes keyboard ornament study
sub: Alessandro Marcello → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: an oboe concerto becomes keyboard ornament study alessandro marcello → johann sebastian bach · documented ext the source of bach’s bwv 974 is the d-minor oboe concerto by alessandro marcello, not his brother benedetto. bach recast the oboe-and-strings texture for one keyboard, preserving its italian identity while elaborating the ornamented solo line. oboe concerto in d minor, s d935 keyboard concerto in d minor, bwv 974 (c. 1713–14)

title: A Stabat mater becomes a German psalm
sub: Giovanni Battista Pergolesi → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: a stabat mater becomes a german psalm giovanni battista pergolesi → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach adapted pergolesi’s stabat mater to a german paraphrase of psalm 51 in tilge, hochster, meine sunden, bwv 1083. the music crosses both language and liturgical context: a latin marian text gives way to a german penitential psalm. stabat mater tilge, hochster, meine sunden, bwv 1083 (1740s)

title: Luther’s hymn becomes a contrapuntal fortress
sub: Martin Luther → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: luther’s hymn becomes a contrapuntal fortress martin luther → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach expanded an earlier weimar cantata into a leipzig reformation cantata using luther’s ein feste burg. in the opening movement the chorale appears in long notes in the instrumental parts while the chorus works around it in imitation; the hymn supplies a structural layer, not just a closing quotation. ein feste burg ist unser gott ein feste burg ist unser gott, bwv 80, leipzig versions

title: An old Credo intonation enters Bach’s counterpoint
sub: Gregorian chant → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: an old credo intonation enters bach’s counterpoint gregorian chant → johann sebastian bach · documented ext bach based the opening of the b-minor mass’s credo on an older chant intonation for the words credo in unum deum. he gives the borrowed head-motif measured rhythm and sets it over a walking continuo bass, joining an archaic vocal subject to an active instrumental foundation. plainchant intonation, credo in unum deum mass in b minor, bwv 232, opening credo

title: Couperin enters the Bach family notebook
sub: François Couperin → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: couperin enters the bach family notebook francois couperin → johann sebastian bach · documented ext the rondeau in b♭ major entered as no. 6 in the 1725 anna magdalena notebook is couperin’s les bergeries, published in 1717. its presence documents french harpsichord music in the bach household, but does not make the piece bach’s composition or establish him as this entry’s copyist. les bergeries, second livre, sixieme ordre (1717) anna magdalena bach’s 1725 notebook, no. 6, bwv anh. 183

title: Zachow joins counterpoint to foreign repertory
sub: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow → George Frideric Handel · documented
k: zachow joins counterpoint to foreign repertory friedrich wilhelm zachow → george frideric handel · documented ext handel studied with the halle organist friedrich wilhelm zachow before his later hamburg apprenticeship. zachow’s teaching combined counterpoint and figured bass with exposure to italian and french instrumental music, an unusually concrete basis for handel’s later command of several national styles. zachow’s teaching in halle handel’s childhood training

title: Milton’s opposed poems alternate inside Handel’s ode
sub: John Milton → George Frideric Handel · documented
k: milton’s opposed poems alternate inside handel’s ode john milton → george frideric handel · documented ext charles jennens selected and interleaved passages from milton’s companion poems for handel’s l’allegro, il penseroso ed il moderato, first performed in london on 27 february 1740. the third part, il moderato, is jennens’s addition, not a third milton poem: literary adaptation is built into the musical alternation of temperaments. l’allegro and il penseroso l’allegro, il penseroso ed il moderato (1740)

title: Dryden’s musical feast reaches Covent Garden
sub: John Dryden → George Frideric Handel · documented
k: dryden’s musical feast reaches covent garden john dryden → george frideric handel · documented ext the covent garden advertisement for 19 february 1736 announces a new ode written by the late dryden and set by handel. a letter of 24 january already describes handel playing almost the entire new work to shaftesbury, who singled out the chorus beginning ‘happy, happy’: contemporary witnesses identify both the literary source and the composition in preparation. alexander’s feast, or the power of musick alexander’s feast, hwv 75 (1736)

title: A Roman keyboard contest survives as anecdote
sub: George Frideric Handel → Domenico Scarlatti · disputed
k: a roman keyboard contest survives as anecdote george frideric handel → domenico scarlatti · disputed ext the familiar account places handel and scarlatti in a keyboard contest at cardinal ottoboni’s in rome, with handel preferred on the organ. the story belongs to the retrospective anecdotal tradition surrounding their italian encounters; it is evidence of how their reputations were narrated, not proof that a particular scarlatti sonata borrows from handel. handel’s keyboard playing in italy scarlatti’s reported encounter with handel

title: Emanuel identifies his only music teacher
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach · documented
k: emanuel identifies his only music teacher johann sebastian bach → carl philipp emanuel bach · documented ext in the autobiography prepared for burney and published in 1773, emanuel bach identifies his father as his only teacher of composition and keyboard playing. the same document lists his first published keyboard minuet in 1731; the teaching link rests on the pupil’s own testimony, not merely their surname. johann sebastian bach’s household teaching c. p. e. bach’s training in keyboard and composition

title: Haydn learns at the keyboard from Emanuel
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn learns at the keyboard from emanuel carl philipp emanuel bach → joseph haydn · documented ext haydn recalled playing emanuel bach’s sonatas repeatedly during his early years of independent study. the testimony names actual keyboard works as models; it does not say that haydn was emanuel’s personal pupil or identify one particular sonata as the source of a later haydn theme. c. p. e. bach’s keyboard sonatas haydn’s independent keyboard studies

title: Palestrina becomes a counterpoint teacher on paper
sub: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina → Johann Joseph Fux · documented
k: palestrina becomes a counterpoint teacher on paper giovanni pierluigi da palestrina → johann joseph fux · documented ext fux’s gradus ad parnassum presents counterpoint through a dialogue between aloysius, representing palestrina, and josephus, representing fux. the imagined lesson became a route from the older contrapuntal ideal into the studies of haydn and beethoven; it is not a historical claim that fux met palestrina. palestrina’s reputation as a contrapuntal model gradus ad parnassum (1725)

title: Haydn works Fux’s problems more than once
sub: Johann Joseph Fux → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn works fux’s problems more than once johann joseph fux → joseph haydn · documented ext griesinger’s account, reproduced by nohl, describes haydn solving fux’s counterpoint problems, putting them aside, then returning to check them. the method was repeated written work rather than a single encounter with a famous treatise, and haydn retained a worn copy. gradus ad parnassum (1725) haydn’s self-directed counterpoint exercises

title: Accompanying singing lessons teaches Haydn declamation
sub: Nicola Antonio Porpora → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: accompanying singing lessons teaches haydn declamation nicola antonio porpora → joseph haydn · documented ext in vienna, haydn accompanied pupils in porpora’s singing lessons and received instruction in return. porpora’s teaching connected composition with singing and italian declamation, a practical complement to haydn’s independent keyboard and counterpoint studies. porpora’s vocal and compositional teaching in vienna haydn’s lessons in the early 1750s

title: Haydn hears Handel’s London festival scale
sub: George Frideric Handel → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn hears handel’s london festival scale george frideric handel → joseph haydn · documented ext during his first london visit, haydn attended the handel commemoration at the end of may 1791. hearing handel’s choral music in this setting preceded haydn’s later english-inspired oratorios; the encounter is firmer evidence than treating every large haydn chorus as a borrowing from messiah. handel’s music at the london commemoration haydn’s london experience in 1791

title: Haydn hears Mozart’s new quartets at home
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn hears mozart’s new quartets at home wolfgang amadeus mozart → joseph haydn · documented ext mozart played his six new quartets for haydn in vienna on 15 january 1785; the newest three were heard again at mozart’s home on 12 february. leopold’s report of the second gathering preserves haydn’s strong approval, documenting direct listening rather than an inferred general kinship between their quartet styles. quartets k. 387, 421, 428, 458, 464 and 465 haydn’s hearings in vienna, january–february 1785

title: Six quartets are entrusted to Haydn
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: six quartets are entrusted to haydn wolfgang amadeus mozart → joseph haydn · documented ext artaria’s first edition of mozart’s six quartets carries an italian dedication to haydn. the dedication is a separate piece of evidence from possible op. 33 modelling: it is an explicit published acknowledgement, while the precise extent of that musical modelling is left open in the critical edition’s foreword. six string quartets, k. 387–465 dedication to joseph haydn in artaria’s 1785 edition

title: Bach’s keyboard sonatas become Mozart concertos
sub: Johann Christian Bach → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: bach’s keyboard sonatas become mozart concertos johann christian bach → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented ext mozart’s three concertos k. 107 transform johann christian bach’s op. 5 nos. 2, 3 and 4 into works for keyboard with strings. the surviving manuscript contains work by both wolfgang and leopold, so these arrangements document a practical family workshop in concerto writing as well as wolfgang’s admiration for the london bach. keyboard sonatas op. 5 nos. 2–4 three keyboard concertos, k. 107 (after 1770)

title: Emanuel’s miniature supplies a concerto finale
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: emanuel’s miniature supplies a concerto finale carl philipp emanuel bach → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented ext the finale of mozart’s k. 40 reworks emanuel bach’s keyboard piece la boehmer. leopold dated the concerto manuscript july 1767, and the critical edition identifies this specific source: the bach connection here is an actual pasticcio movement, not a general claim about mozart’s expressive style. la boehmer, published in musikalisches allerley (1761) keyboard concerto in d major, k. 40, finale (july 1767)

title: Bach’s keyboard fugues acquire string voices
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: bach’s keyboard fugues acquire string voices johann sebastian bach → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented ext mozart arranged five bach fugues for two violins, viola and cello in the group traditionally numbered k. 405. the critical edition places the bach arrangements beside the quartet work of 1782; the arrangement itself is secure evidence of study, without proving that every later contrapuntal mozart passage came from bach. fugues from the well-tempered clavier five fugues for string quartet, k. 405 (1782)

title: Sunday sessions bring Bach and Handel home
sub: Gottfried van Swieten → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: sunday sessions bring bach and handel home gottfried van swieten → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented ext in his letter to nannerl of 20 april 1782, mozart explains that van swieten lent him bach and handel works after he had played them at the baron’s sunday gatherings. constanze’s enthusiasm for fugues then helped prompt the prelude and fugue k. 394: the letter supplies a named intermediary and a particular compositional result. van swieten’s bach and handel repertory mozart’s prelude and fugue in c, k. 394 (1782)

title: Mozart recolours Messiah for Viennese winds
sub: George Frideric Handel → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: mozart recolours messiah for viennese winds george frideric handel → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented ext at van swieten’s initiative, mozart arranged handel’s messiah for german-language performances in vienna in 1789. his version adds wind colouring to handel’s texture rather than composing a new oratorio; the arrangement was made for particular performances and appeared in print only after mozart’s death. messiah, hwv 56 (1741) der messias, k. 572 (1789)

title: A Mozart suite looks towards Handel
sub: George Frideric Handel → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · inferred
k: a mozart suite looks towards handel george frideric handel → wolfgang amadeus mozart · inferred ext the critical edition identifies handel’s suites as the principal stylistic model for mozart’s incomplete suite k. 399. its overture, allemande and courante belong to mozart’s 1782 engagement with older keyboard music; the unfinished sarabande also prevents the fragment from being presented as a completed four-movement suite. handel’s keyboard suites suite k. 399, overture and dances (1782)

title: Haydn teaches Beethoven counterpoint in Vienna
sub: Joseph Haydn → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: haydn teaches beethoven counterpoint in vienna joseph haydn → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven’s lessons with haydn began in early 1793 after his move from bonn to vienna. the exercises drew on fux’s gradus ad parnassum; when haydn left for london in january 1794, beethoven continued contrapuntal study with albrechtsberger. haydn’s counterpoint teaching, based on fux beethoven’s viennese studies, 1793–94

title: Fugue and canon follow Haydn’s departure
sub: Johann Georg Albrechtsberger → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: fugue and canon follow haydn’s departure johann georg albrechtsberger → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext after haydn’s january 1794 departure for london, beethoven took lessons from johann georg albrechtsberger. the subjects were counterpoint, fugue and canon, making this a different documented stage of training from the italian vocal work he later undertook with salieri. albrechtsberger’s teaching of counterpoint, fugue and canon beethoven’s studies in 1794

title: Salieri teaches Beethoven Italian vocal style
sub: Antonio Salieri → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: salieri teaches beethoven italian vocal style antonio salieri → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven studied italian vocal and operatic style with antonio salieri around 1800–02. these lessons concerned writing for the voice, rather than replacing the counterpoint training beethoven had already received from haydn and albrechtsberger. salieri’s instruction in italian vocal writing beethoven’s lessons, around 1800–02

title: Beethoven copies fugues to teach an archduke
sub: Johann Joseph Fux → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: beethoven copies fugues to teach an archduke johann joseph fux → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven’s autograph hcb mh 45 copies two four-part fugues from fux’s gradus ad parnassum. beethoven-haus relates the copy, probably, to the compendium he prepared for archduke rudolph’s theoretical lessons: the older textbook passes through beethoven to another pupil. gradus ad parnassum: two four-part fugues beethoven’s autograph study material, hcb mh 45

title: The Well-Tempered Clavier enters Beethoven’s early training
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: the well-tempered clavier enters beethoven’s early training johann sebastian bach → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven studied bach’s well-tempered clavier as a young keyboard player in bonn. this is an early educational connection, distinct from later attempts to identify bach quotations in beethoven’s late fugues. the well-tempered clavier beethoven’s keyboard studies in bonn

title: Beethoven copies Emanuel while studying with Haydn
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: beethoven copies emanuel while studying with haydn carl philipp emanuel bach → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext during his viennese studies in 1793–94, beethoven copied keyboard sonatas by emanuel bach. other surviving extracts come from emanuel’s versuch uber die wahre art das clavier zu spielen, which beethoven also used when teaching his own pupils. c. p. e. bach’s keyboard sonatas and versuch beethoven’s copies and theoretical extracts

title: Handel’s conquering hero becomes chamber variations
sub: George Frideric Handel → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: handel’s conquering hero becomes chamber variations george frideric handel → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven used handel’s ‘see, the conqu’ring hero comes’ as the theme of twelve variations for cello and piano, woo 45, in 1796. his surviving study copies also include passages from handel’s messiah in mozart’s arrangement: borrowing a recognisable tune and copying a score are two separately documented forms of his engagement with handel. see, the conqu’ring hero comes, judas maccabaeus twelve variations for cello and piano, woo 45 (1796)

title: Beethoven studies Mozart’s ensembles for Fidelio
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: beethoven studies mozart’s ensembles for fidelio wolfgang amadeus mozart → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext while beginning work on fidelio, beethoven copied passages from mozart’s don giovanni to study the handling of vocal ensembles. beethoven-haus exhibited this study manuscript: the mechanism is written compositional analysis, not the unverified story that mozart personally taught beethoven in 1787. don giovanni: ensemble passages beethoven’s study copy during work on fidelio

title: Schiller’s ode enters a symphonic finale
sub: Friedrich Schiller → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: schiller’s ode enters a symphonic finale friedrich schiller → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven incorporated schiller’s an die freude in the choral finale of the ninth symphony, first performed in vienna on 7 may 1824. the literary connection belongs to the sung finale, not to a retrospective programme imposed on the instrumental movements. an die freude symphony no. 9, finale (1824) ode-to-joy

title: Goethe’s tragedy receives Beethoven’s stage music
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: goethe’s tragedy receives beethoven’s stage music johann wolfgang von goethe → ludwig van beethoven · documented ext beethoven composed music for goethe’s egmont in 1809–10, including songs, entr’actes and music for the tragedy’s final act. he announced the work to goethe by letter in 1811, before their personal meetings in 1812; the setting therefore did not result from a collaboration begun at teplitz. egmont incidental music to egmont, op. 84 (1809–10)

title: Schubert’s early compositions lead to Salieri lessons
k: schubert’s early compositions lead to salieri lessons antonio salieri → franz schubert · documented ext schubert’s early compositional gifts led to study with antonio salieri in vienna. the link joins schubert to a working vocal composer and teacher, rather than to the fictional account of salieri as mozart’s murderer. salieri’s compositional teaching in vienna schubert’s early musical training

title: Faust’s spinning scene becomes a piano song
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Franz Schubert · documented
k: faust’s spinning scene becomes a piano song johann wolfgang von goethe → franz schubert · documented ext schubert set goethe’s gretchen text as gretchen am spinnrade, d. 118, in 1814. gibbs places it beside erlkonig among the early goethe settings that made the piano an active interpreter of the poem, rather than treating it as a neutral support for the voice. faust: gretchen’s song gretchen am spinnrade, d. 118 (1814)

title: Goethe’s ballad becomes Schubert’s first published opus
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Franz Schubert · documented
k: goethe’s ballad becomes schubert’s first published opus johann wolfgang von goethe → franz schubert · documented ext schubert composed his setting of goethe’s erlkonig, d. 328, in 1815; it later became his op. 1. the pairing of a specific poem, catalogue number and publication identity makes this a direct literary inheritance, not a loose association with german romantic poetry. erlkonig erlkonig, d. 328, op. 1 (1815)

title: Schubert carries a torch for Beethoven
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Franz Schubert · documented
k: schubert carries a torch for beethoven ludwig van beethoven → franz schubert · documented ext schubert was a torchbearer in beethoven’s funeral procession on 29 march 1827. this public act of homage is documented separately from uncertain stories of bedside visits, and does not imply that the two men had enjoyed a sustained personal friendship. beethoven’s public memorial in vienna schubert at the funeral, 29 march 1827
